items.explanation: Unrestricted U-boat warfare, the Lusitania sinking, and the Zimmermann Telegram all pushed America toward war — but the 1916 Sussex Pledge was Germany promising restraint, the one step away from war.
options: C. The sinking of the Lusitania
items.stem: All of the following moved America toward war with Germany EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. The 1916 Sussex Pledge was Germany's promise to limit submarine warfare and warn merchant ships — a step back from war, not toward it. It was the one move that eased tensions rather than inflaming them.
option_explanations.B: Germany's 1917 return to unrestricted U-boat warfare — sinking ships without warning — was the final provocation that pushed Wilson to ask for war. It moved America toward war, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: The 1915 sinking of the Lusitania, killing 128 Americans, outraged the United States and moved it toward war. It is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The 1917 Zimmermann Telegram — Germany's offer of an alliance to Mexico against the U.S. — inflamed American opinion and moved the country toward war. It is not the exception.

items.explanation: Wilson dreamed of a democratic peace, but Clemenceau's France wanted Germany crippled — reparations, territory, and security — clashing fundamentally with the Fourteen Points.
options: A. They opposed any League of Nations
B. They resented Germany's exclusion from peacemaking
D. They wanted to punish Germany, not reform the world
items.stem: France opposed much of Wilson's Fourteen Points because

option_explanations.A: France did not oppose the League as such — France actually wanted a strong alliance system for security against Germany. French objections were about the peace's terms, not about the League existing.
option_explanations.B: France had no wish to include Germany in peacemaking — Clemenceau wanted Germany excluded and punished. Resenting Germany's exclusion would have been Germany's complaint, not France's.
option_explanations.C: Clemenceau and Wilson clashed personally, but personal disdain was not the basis of French opposition. France's objection was substantive: it wanted security through a weakened Germany, not through Wilson's ideals.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Wilson dreamed of a democratic peace that would reform the world, but Clemenceau's France wanted Germany crippled — reparations, lost territory, military limits. France's demand for punishment clashed fundamentally with the Fourteen Points' vision.

items.explanation: The home front mobilized through Liberty Bond drives — with stars like Chaplin and Fairbanks headlining rallies — plus the draft, war industries, and propaganda. There were no ration cards or German-American camps.
options: A. Ration cards went to every family
B. German-Americans were herded into camps
C. Cities drilled for enemy attack
D. Celebrities helped sell Liberty Bonds

option_explanations.A: There were no general ration cards for American families in World War I — food conservation was voluntary ('Meatless Mondays,' 'Wheatless Wednesdays'), not rationed. Ration cards came in World War II.
option_explanations.B: German-Americans faced intense suspicion and harassment, but they were not herded into camps. Internment camps were a World War II policy against Japanese-Americans, not a World War I policy against German-Americans.
option_explanations.C: American cities did not drill for enemy attack in 1917 — the war was an ocean away and German bombers could not reach the U.S. Air-raid drills belong to later wars.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The home front mobilized through Liberty Bond drives — with celebrities like Charlie Chaplin and Douglas Fairbanks headlining rallies — plus the draft, war industries, and propaganda. There were no ration cards or German-American internment camps.

items.explanation: Lodge offered reservations -- especially protecting Congress's war power against Article X -- that a majority of senators could accept. Wilson, shattered by his stroke and rigid in idealism, ordered loyal Democrats to vote against the treaty with reservations attached, defeating his own League rather than compromising.
options: A. He refused to accept Lodge's reservations to the treaty
B. The American people opposed any peace treaty at all
C. The League of Nations was never formally proposed
D. Senate Republicans united behind Wilson's version
items.stem: Wilson's campaign for the League of Nations failed in the Senate primarily because
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"You may call me selfish if you will, conservative or reactionary, or use any other harsh adjective you see fit to apply, but an American I was born, an American I have remained all my life. I can never be anything else."
—Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, 1919 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Lodge offered reservations — especially protecting Congress's war power against Article X — that a Senate majority could accept. Wilson, shattered by his stroke and rigid in his idealism, ordered loyal Democrats to vote against the treaty with the reservations attached, defeating his own League rather than compromising.
option_explanations.B: The American people did not oppose any peace treaty — the country wanted peace and many supported the League. The failure was in the Senate, driven by Wilson's refusal to compromise on the reservations.
option_explanations.C: The League of Nations was formally proposed — in the Treaty of Versailles, which Wilson signed and brought home. The proposal was real; it was Wilson's all-or-nothing stance that killed it in the Senate.
option_explanations.D: Senate Republicans did not unite behind Wilson's version — Lodge led the opposition precisely to force reservations on the treaty. It was the Democrats, following Wilson's orders, who voted down the treaty with reservations.
